extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, literary critics, and educated readers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for judging poems and poets: assessing diction, imagination, sincerity, originality, temperament, and the proper conduct of critics. Includes warnings about common faults in modern verse and about misattributing irritability to genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine admiration should be continuous and understated
rubrics_metrics.description: Our genuine admiration of a great poet is a continuous undercurrent of feeling; it is everywhere present, but seldom anywhere as a separate excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obvious, showy marks of the author's self-admiration (e.g., forced exclamations or conspicuous flourishes). Great poetry evokes a steady, pervasive sense of admiration rather than isolated clever effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision and necessity of diction in great poets
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be scarcely more difficult ... to alter a word, or the position of a word, in Milton or Shakespeare ... without making the poet say something else, or something worse, than he does say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every word in a great poet's line is necessary; strive for exactness of word choice and resist gratuitous substitutions that change meaning or weaken effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural thought combined with natural diction (reconcile heart and head)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowper and Bowles were ... the first who combined natural thoughts with natural diction; the first who reconciled the heart with the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value unity between feeling and expression: thoughts should arise naturally from emotions and the diction should match that naturalness rather than being artificially ornate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sacrificing feeling to wit or to mere ornament (heart vs head vs drapery)
rubrics_metrics.description: The faulty elder poets sacrificed the passion ... to the subtleties of intellect and to the stars of wit; the moderns to the glare and glitter of a perpetual, yet broken and heterogeneous imagery ... The one sacrificed the heart to the head; the other both heart and head to point and drapery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let technical cleverness, epigrammatic points, or flashy imagery replace genuine emotion and coherent thought. Beware heterogeneous or 'amphibious' images that are half image/half abstract meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three poetic sins to avoid (risu honesto)
rubrics_metrics.description: The three sins of poetry ... (1) doleful egotism, and recurrence of favourite phrases, with the double defect of being at once trite and licentious; (2) low creeping language and thoughts, under the pretence of simplicity; (3) the indiscriminate use of elaborate and swelling language and imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid (1) sentimental, self-pitying egotism and repetitive catch-phrases; (2) false/simple language that masks poverty of thought; (3) indiscriminate grandiose diction and inflated imagery that aren't earned by content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reforms and stylistic corrections must avoid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Every reform, however necessary, will by weak minds be carried to an excess, which will itself need reforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing style or correcting faults, aim for balance; do not swing from one extreme to another—excessive simplicity or excessive ornament are both faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate irritability with genius; investigate causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A charge of irritability brought against men of genius is often unjust: irritability may originate in ill conformation of body, obtuse pain, or constitutional defect of pleasurable sensation rather than genius itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an author's temperament, consider health, circumstances, and psychology rather than assuming that sharpness or testiness is an intrinsic mark of genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: True genius tends to calmness and indifference to immediate fame
rubrics_metrics.description: The men of the greatest genius ... appear to have been of calm and tranquil temper in all that related to themselves. In the inward assurance of permanent fame, they seem to have been either indifferent or resigned with regard to immediate reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect seriousness and steadiness of temperament in great writers; extravagant vanity or petty vindictiveness is not a reliable sign of high poetic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination should blend feelings with ideas; interest in thoughts over things
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the ideas are vivid, ... the feelings and affections blend more easily and intimately with these ideal creations than with the objects of the senses; the mind is affected by thoughts, rather than by things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a poet's imagination by how seamlessly feeling and conceptual thought are integrated; superior poetry moves the reader through idealized thought-forms rather than merely sensory description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish works of genius from mechanized, manufactured verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Now ... language, mechanized as it were into a barrel-organ, supplies at once both instrument and tune. Thus even the deaf may play ... of all modes of literature, the manufacturing of poems. The difference indeed between these and the works of genius is not less than between an egg and an egg-shell; yet at a distance they both look alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware poems that imitate form without substance—clever surface tricks that spare the reader thought. Value depth, originality, and inner vitality over facile, repeatable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critics should argue fully and responsibly, not in passing or anonymously
rubrics_metrics.description: If I should ever deem it my duty ... I would oppose them in books which could be weighed and answered, in which I could evolve the whole of my reasons and feelings ... not in irrecoverable conversation ... As long as there are readers to be delighted with calumny, there will be found reviewers to calumniate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate criticism is thorough, accountable, and presented where it can be engaged with and answered; casual, anonymous, or malicious attacks are disreputable and distort public judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praises of the unworthy harm the deserving
rubrics_metrics.description: Praises of the unworthy are felt by ardent minds as robberies of the deserving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical discernment matters: elevating inferior work (through fashion, party spirit, or malice) deprives truly meritorious writers of recognition and misleads readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors have legitimate claims to protection and measured self-defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a man has ... devoted his whole being to an object ... what of all that relates to himself and his family ... can have fairer claims to his protection, or more authorize acts of self-defence, than the elaborate products of his intellect and intellectual industry?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect an author's stake in his work; measured responses to gross provocation are legitimate, and prudence dictates some degree of protective concern for one’s intellectual offspring.
